commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether negotiating liability, indemnification, and disclosure terms in AI vendor contracts reduces unexpected risk shifting or suppression of harm reports, and no study documents the hazard itself. Support for the practice rests on five endorsements, four of them frameworks or guidance and one a commentary.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Five sources endorse it, two at the must level. One must-level source, the augmented intelligence principles, addresses human review before care denials rather than contract terms, so it bears only indirectly on this recommendation. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

The endorsing sources are voluntary frameworks from CHAI and NIST, which carry no legal force. The NIST generative AI profile asks organizations to review vendor contracts for non-standard terms that may amplify or defer liability in unexpected ways. None of the supplied sources cites a statute or regulation that prohibits gag clauses in AI vendor contracts.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that catalog liability, indemnification, and confidentiality terms in executed health care AI contracts and that compare incident disclosure and cost allocation between organizations that negotiated these terms and those that accepted vendor defaults.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net organizations may have less negotiating capacity with vendors, and whether they can secure these terms remains unknown.
